Vancomycin is likely to be the antibacterial of choice in penicillin-allergic patients requir- ing empirical treatment,5 and may be used empirically with an aminoglycoside in patients with prosthetic valves or where penicillin resistance is suspected.4,6 (UK guide- lines also add rifampicin in these situations.6) Once the causative organism and its antibiotic susceptibil- ity have been identified, appropriate pathogen-directed therapy may be begun. • Streptococcal endocarditis. Streptococci vary in their susceptibility to penicillin, and guidelines generally di- vide regimens according to whether the organism is of low, intermediate, or high penicillin resistance, although at what MIC these categories are defined varies between guidelines. For uncomplicated cases of infection with the most pen- icillin sensitive streptococci, benzylpenicillin may be used, with or without gentamicin.4-8 Typically, if used alone in native-valve infection it would be given for 4 weeks, whereas the combination regimen is given only for 2 weeks.6-8 Indicative doses would be 1.2 to 2.4 g of benzylpenicillin every 4 hours, and gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours. Ceftriaxone or vancomycin may be con- sidered as an alternative,6 although these are more often given to treat less sensitive strains, or in patients unable to tolerate penicillin. For streptococci less sensitive to penicillin benzylpeni- cillin may be given as above but for 4 to 6 weeks,4,6,7 usually with gentamicin for at least the first 2 weeks. Alternatively, 4 weeks of treatment with ceftriaxone or vancomycin may be considered.6-8 Typical doses are 2 g daily of ceftriaxone as a single injection, or 30 mg/kg of vancomycin daily (up to a usual maximum of 2 g daily), in 2 divided doses. For penicillin resistant streptococci treatment is similar to that for enterococcal endocarditis.6,7 A combination of vancomycin and gentamicin may be given for 4 to 6 weeks. Streptomycin is a possible alternative to gen- tamicin for gentamicin resistant isolates.6 For streptococci in penicillin-allergic patients, vanco- mycin for 4 to 6 weeks may be given; UK guidelines advise 4 weeks of treatment combined with gentamicin for the first 2 weeks.6 Teicoplanin, typically in doses of 6 to 10 mg/kg daily (higher loading doses should be giv- en initially to establish a suitable trough concentration) is a possible alternative to vancomycin.6 Some patients may tolerate ceftriaxone.4 For patients with prosthetic valve endocarditis, a regi- men similar to that for less sensitive streptococci (above) has been suggested, given for at least 6 weeks.6-8 • Staphylococcal endocarditis.
